paragraphs: Your model will learn whatever your dataset says, including its accidents. A training row can carry a customer's credentials, a citation to a policy that doesn't exist, or the very test you were saving for release day. None of that shows up in a loss curve.

So before any training starts, each record needs a job. An approved answer gives the model something to imitate. A comparison says which of two answers is better. A reserved case tests a future model. A failure becomes an incident to investigate. Mix those up, and you end up training on your own exam.

You'll route records by hand, measure whether two reviewers agree beyond chance, and work out where the next hour of review should go. All of it runs on small examples you can check with a calculator.
By the end you'll have a dataset where every row can say why it's there. That's what the next chapter trains on.
outcomes: Route each record to training, evaluation, or incident review, and say why.
Read reviewer agreement with its counts, then use disagreement to fix the rubric.
Test whether a smarter selector beats random sampling without spending your test set.
question: If a colleague picked one row from your dataset at random, could they tell why it's there?
